title: "Signage panels for platform displays — field research summary"
created: 2025-10-24
provenance: generated
tags: [embedded, field-research]
source: "internal field research summary"
---

High-brightness signage panels promise sunlight readability on paper; field
experience says viewing angle and heat are the real costs, and one board per
display keeps wiring simple until firmware updates land. Expect manual
reflash cycles and clock sets when boards run unattended.

Informed the original Perchboard per-display architecture (d-103).

line for both.

Single-board computers at one per display promise autonomy: no central
server, local fallback rendering, simple wiring. Field experience says
flashing and clock drift are the real costs — expect manual reflash cycles
when firmware updates land.

Informed the original Wayfare per-display architecture (d-003).

---
id: fleet-provisioning-notes
genre: references
title: "Provisioning device fleets — ops note"
created: 2026-04-06
provenance: hand-authored
tags: [infrastructure, ops-note]
source: "internal ops note"
related:
  - type: relates_to
    to: references/embedded-single-board-notes.md
---

Provisioning a fleet of small boards two ways: point-wise flashing scales
linearly with board count and fails quietly; a gateway-hub topology flashes
once per site and funnels telemetry home. The hub costs one more box per
station but collapses the maintenance surface.

Written after the Wayfare field pain (s-004); the hub topology is the
direction d-008 adopted.

Perchboard is Copperleaf Studio's realtime departure-display program for
Bayline Transit: platform displays for three pilot stations — Granite Pier,
Tram Junction, Lighthouse Point — fed by live vehicle-position data.

Scope agreed at the kickoff (2025-09-29) with Dara Whitlock: sub-second
perceived freshness, outdoor readability, and a May ship date. The displays
speak MQTT 5.0 (decision d-102) and went from per-display autonomy (d-103)
to an edge relay per station (d-109) after field maintenance pain. The
palette is high-contrast white-on-black (d-112), with fleet clocks kept
honest by chrony (d-110).
